name: John Calvin
role: French Reformer, theologian, and pastor of Geneva

died.cause: Illness after a long decline (tuberculosis and other ailments)

summary: French theologian whose Institutes of the Christian Religion and work in Geneva shaped the Reformed and Presbyterian churches.

key_dates.label: Flees Paris after Nicolas Cop's reforming address of 1 November; his conversion is usually dated c. 1533
First edition of the Institutes (Basel, March); settles in Geneva at William Farel's urging
Expelled from Geneva with Farel (April); goes to Strasbourg
Marries Idelette de Bure in Strasbourg
Returns to Geneva (September); the Ecclesiastical Ordinances set up the Consistory
Michael Servetus burned in Geneva (27 October)
Opponents in the city council defeated; Calvin's supporters take control of Geneva
Final Latin edition of the Institutes; founds the Genevan Academy

accomplishments.text: Wrote the Institutes of the Christian Religion, expanded from a short handbook (1536) to a full system of theology (1559), the most influential work of Reformed Protestant theology.

Organized the Genevan church under the Ecclesiastical Ordinances (1541), with pastors, teachers, elders, and deacons, and a Consistory that disciplined moral conduct; the model spread to France, Scotland, the Netherlands, and beyond.
Taught God's sovereignty in salvation, including double predestination, which became a defining doctrine of Reformed theology.
Wrote commentaries on most of the Bible and preached several times a week in Geneva for over two decades.
Served as pastor to French refugees in Strasbourg (1538–41), where he worked with Martin Bucer and took part in religious colloquies with Catholic and Lutheran theologians.
Founded the Genevan Academy (1559), which trained pastors sent into France; Geneva sent over 100 ministers to France by 1562.
Wrote against the Council of Trent in Acts of the Council of Trent with the Antidote (1547).

Pressed the heresy prosecution of Michael Servetus, who was burned in Geneva in 1553, and defended the execution in print; he had earlier supplied evidence that helped the Catholic Inquisition at Vienne prosecute Servetus.

Supported the Geneva Consistory's strict enforcement of morals and the punishment of opponents, including the execution of Jacques Gruet (1547) and the banishment of Jerome Bolsec (1551) for attacking his teaching on predestination.

original.phrase: Man's nature, so to speak, is a perpetual factory of idols.
God by a sudden conversion subdued and brought my mind to a teachable frame.
original.reference: Preface to the Commentary on the Psalms (1557)

misattributed.phrase: TULIP (Total depravity, Unconditional election, Limited atonement, Irresistible grace, Perseverance of the saints)
misattributed.note: Not Calvin's. The five points come from the Synod of Dort (1618–19), after his death, and the TULIP acrostic dates from the early 20th century.

victims_title: People executed in Geneva linked to Calvin
victims_intro: The Geneva city councils, not Calvin, held the power to try and execute; Calvin was a pastor and, until 1559, not even a citizen. These are the cases most often laid at his door, with how far his part is documented.

victims.name: Michael Servetus
victims.condemned_by: Small Council of Geneva, after consulting the churches of Zurich, Bern, Basel, and Schaffhausen
victims.allegation: Calvin had his secretary file the charges, led the theological case against Servetus at trial, and defended the execution in his Defence of the Orthodox Faith (1554). He asked for a less cruel death than burning, which the council refused.
victims.verification_note: The trial records and Calvin's own letters and writings document his role.

victims.name: Jacques Gruet
victims.allegation: Gruet was arrested after a threatening placard against the ministers was found on Calvin's pulpit, and tortured; Calvin supported the prosecution.
victims.verification_note: The execution is documented; Calvin's influence on the verdict is argued from his letters and circumstances rather than any direct order.

victims.name: People accused of spreading plague (1545)
victims.executed: About two dozen executed in Geneva, 1545
victims.allegation: During a plague outbreak, people accused of deliberately spreading it with ointments were tortured and executed; Calvin accepted that such a conspiracy existed and did not oppose the prosecutions.
victims.verification_note: The trials are in the city records; Calvin's role was support rather than direction.

persecution_note: Calvin was never imprisoned for his faith (an imprisonment at Noyon in 1534 is sometimes reported but may concern another man of the same name). He fled France during the crackdown on Protestants in 1533–34 and was expelled from Geneva in 1538.

persecution.title: Flight from France
persecution.summary: After the rector Nicolas Cop gave a reforming address at the University of Paris, which Calvin may have helped write, the Parlement of Paris moved against both men and Calvin fled the city. After the Affair of the Placards (October 1534), when anti-Mass posters appeared across France, Francis I's government burned Protestants and Calvin left France for Basel.

responsible.name: Parlement of Paris
responsible.role: Prosecuted those linked to Cop's address

responsible.name: Francis I
responsible.role: King of France; ordered the crackdown after the Placards

persecution.outcome: Exile; he dedicated the 1536 Institutes to Francis I in defense of the persecuted French Protestants.

persecution.title: Expulsion from Geneva
persecution.summary: After Calvin and Farel refused to follow the city's orders on church practice and to give communion while the city was divided, the councils of Geneva gave them three days to leave.

responsible.name: Councils of Geneva (Small Council, Two Hundred, and General Council)

persecution.outcome: Went to Strasbourg; invited back in 1541.

excommunication_note: No papal bull excommunicating Calvin by name is known, but as a Protestant he was outside the Catholic Church and all his works were banned.

excommunications.reason: Calvin listed among authors all of whose works were forbidden to Catholics

persecuted_others_note: Calvin supported the punishment of heretics and opponents by Geneva's councils: he led the prosecution of Michael Servetus and defended his execution in print, and backed the banishment of opponents such as Jerome Bolsec and the punishment of the Perrinist faction. Earlier, in the preface to his Institutes (1536), he had pleaded with the King of France for persecuted French Protestants, and he asked that Servetus be given a less cruel death than burning.

persecuted_others.title: Executions in Geneva linked to him (summary)
persecuted_others.targets: Michael Servetus, Jacques Gruet, and people accused of spreading plague (1545)
persecuted_others.summary: See the list of executed people above. Geneva's councils, not Calvin, tried and sentenced these cases; his part ranged from bringing the charges and leading the case against Servetus to unclear or minor roles in the others. He defended the execution of heretics in his Defence of the Orthodox Faith (1554).

persecuted_others.title: Banishment of Jerome Bolsec
persecuted_others.targets: Jerome Bolsec, former Carmelite and physician who attacked Calvin's doctrine of predestination
persecuted_others.summary: After Bolsec publicly challenged predestination in October 1551, Calvin and the ministers pressed the case against him before the Geneva council, which consulted the other Swiss churches and then banished him for life. Bolsec later returned to Catholicism and wrote a hostile biography of Calvin (1577).

persecuted_others.title: Suppression of the Perrinists
persecuted_others.targets: Ami Perrin and his faction, Calvin's leading political opponents in Geneva
persecuted_others.summary: After a street disturbance in May 1555, the council, now controlled by Calvin's supporters, prosecuted the Perrinist leaders: several were executed and Perrin and others fled and were condemned in their absence. Calvin supported the crackdown, which ended organized opposition to him in Geneva.
